name: The Inner Temple Mulberry

location.address: Benchers' Walk, Inner Temple Garden, by the railings outside Paper Buildings, City of London EC4Y

access: Public, open weekdays 12:30pm-3:00pm only (not full daily access)
verify_notes: Existence and species confirmed by two independent sources: Morus Londinium's Inner Temple survey (heritage/notable mulberry, girth 150cm, height 10m, by the railings of Benchers' Walk outside Paper Buildings) and the Inner Temple's own official garden-history page, which names the black mulberry as one of the survivors of the garden's 'ancient orchard' alongside a large-fruiting walnut and a quince, i.e. the Inner Temple itself frames it as historic rather than ornamental planting. No source gives a planting date or age; black mulberries are notoriously hard to age and can live 200-400+ years, but that is not a substitute for a source, so age_estimate is left undocumented rather than guessed. Coordinates are the garden's approximate centre near Benchers' Walk, not a tree-level pin, hence approximate. Access is real but restricted to a 2.5 hour weekday window, worth stating plainly rather than implying casual walk-up access. This tree sits about 250m from the already-published lon_019 (The Fountain Court Mulberries, Temple) and forms a natural pair/cluster point for a City/Temple walk alongside lon_003 (Cheapside Plane) and lon_011 (St Paul's Churchyard Planes), both roughly 1.2-1.4km away.

name: The Finsbury Circus Pagoda Tree

location.address: Finsbury Circus Gardens, City of London EC2M

access: Free, public garden, standard park hours
transport: Moorgate station, 3 minute walk; Liverpool Street station, 6 minute walk
verify_notes: Existence confirmed as currently standing by the City of London's own official garden page (fetched directly, live copy, present tense): 'The present garden was originally laid out in 1815 to a design by George Dance the Younger. It's well known for its mature London plane trees and fine Japanese Pagoda tree - the only one in the City.' This is the only Japanese Pagoda tree in the City of London per that source. CityAM's feature independently corroborates: 'the City of London's only Japanese Pagoda tree', part of the 1815 redesign. Age is inferential, not a direct planting record: both sources associate the pagoda tree with the 1815 Dance redesign but neither states it was planted that exact year, so age_estimate is given as a range (roughly 200 years) rather than a precise figure, and this should read as circumstantial dating in the story. SURVIVAL CONFIRMED: Finsbury Circus Gardens underwent a major Crossrail-era renovation, closed 2023, reopened May 2025 ('the first major renovation in over 100 years'). The City of London's OWN page, fetched fresh via curl (not cached), describes the pagoda tree in the present tense as a current feature of the garden, which resolves the previous pass's open question about whether it survived the works. Location is garden-level (Finsbury Circus Gardens centre), not a tree-level pin, hence approximate; the garden is compact (2.2 hectares) so a visitor can find it without difficulty. Sits about 0.55km from lon_003 (The Cheapside Plane) and roughly 1.1km from lon_011 (St Paul's Churchyard Planes), extending the City of London cluster north.

name: The Quaker Garden Planes

location.address: Quaker Gardens, between Banner Street and Chequer Street, Islington EC1Y

access: Free, public recreation ground (laid out 1965 within the GLC Banner Street estate), entered from Banner Street or Chequer Street
verify_notes: Existence and species confirmed by two independent sources. Bunhill Fields Quaker Meeting's own site (bunhillquakers.org.uk/garden/) states the garden holds 'several mature London Plane trees planted about 1880' (roughly 145 years). A second source, a local health-walks blog citing the London Gardens Trust inventory record, describes '3 notable plane trees, two of which may be C18th' (roughly 250+ years), which would make them considerably older. SOURCES CONFLICT ON AGE and this pass could not resolve it: the fuller London Gardens Trust inventory record (ISL064) that would likely settle this returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, same as the previous pass. Delivering with the Quaker Meeting's own figure (1880) as the primary age_estimate because it is the site's own institutional history rather than a secondhand blog claim, but this is stated, not silently chosen: a future pass should try ISL064 via a browser session or Wayback Machine to adjudicate. The garden sits on the site of the historic Quaker burial ground (1661-1855) where George Fox, founder of the Religious Society of Friends, was buried in 1691; the trees themselves postdate the burial ground's closure. This is a genuinely public, signposted park (not the adjacent, larger Bunhill Fields Burial Ground, which is a separate already-blocked entry). Sits about 1.4km from lon_012 (The Amwell Street Fig, Clerkenwell), extending that cluster.

name: The Ravenscourt Park Tree of Heaven

location.address: Near the sports area and children's playground, Ravenscourt Park, Hammersmith W6

transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)
verify_notes: Existence, species and its 'largest of its kind' status confirmed by two independent sources. Wikipedia's Great Trees of London table (sourced to Paul Wood's Great Trees of London Map, Blue Crow Media 2020) lists it at tree-level coordinates 51.496330,-0.237089, describing it as 'one of the largest trees of heaven in Britain'. Independently, londontreesblog.wordpress.com describes the on-site circular green plaque itself, which reads 'one of the largest examples of this tree species in the country and one of the Great Trees of London'; a third source, graftingardeners.co.uk, calls it 'the tallest tree of its kind in the country' and says it appears in the Royal Forestry Society/Tree Register's Champion Tree database. No source anywhere gives a planting date or age estimate, only size superlatives, and the species is normally short-lived (londontreesblog cites 'rarely lives more than 50 years'), which makes any age guess unsafe. Never fabricate: age_estimate is left undocumented rather than guessed; the entry qualifies on the visually-spectacular / historically-significant test instead of age. This is genuinely a cheap cluster addition: the coordinate sits about 150m from the already-published lon_018 (The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane, 51.4967/-0.2386, also a Great Trees of London entry in the same park), so this pass effectively doubles Ravenscourt Park's collectible point without any new travel for a visitor.
